matiere: Intro to ML · Python for Data Science · Supervised Learning · Training Process · Metrics · Cross-validation · KNN · Regression

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: Which statement matches the course definition of data science?
choix: Drawing charts of a dataset for managers without any processing
Using automated techniques to analyse vast data and extract knowledge
Writing explicit rules by hand so a computer can process a dataset
Storing very large datasets across many computers in a cluster
questions.explication: Data science involves utilizing automated techniques to analyze vast amounts of data and extract valuable knowledge from it.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: What is the key difference between data analysis and data analytics?
choix: Analysis is a human activity; analytics automates the insights
Analysis needs big data; analytics works only on small datasets
Analysis uses machine learning; analytics only uses spreadsheets
Analysis is always automated; analytics is done by a human expert
questions.explication: Data analysis stands for human activities aimed at gaining insight; data analytics automates insights with queries, aggregation and data mining.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: A Forex trader relies on experience to open or close a position. In the course this is an example of:
questions.explication: The course uses the Forex trader as an example of data analysis: a human activity that can be done without special data processing.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: Automatically discovering non-obvious associations between user purchases is an example of:
questions.explication: Data analytics automates insights and can use data-mining techniques to discover hidden patterns, such as purchase associations.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: How does the course define Big Data?
choix: Data volumes that traditional applications cannot handle efficiently
Data that has already been cleaned and aggregated for reporting
Data stored in a relational database with a fixed table schema
Any dataset that contains more than one million numeric records
questions.explication: Big Data refers to massive volumes of data that traditional applications cannot efficiently handle; it often cannot fit in the memory of one computer.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: How many bytes are in one petabyte, in the decimal units used by the course?
questions.explication: Kilo 10^3, mega 10^6, giga 10^9, tera 10^12, peta 10^15, exa 10^18, zetta 10^21, yotta 10^24.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: Which unit comes directly after the exabyte?
questions.explication: The order is ... petabyte, exabyte, zettabyte, yottabyte.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: Which of the 5 Vs of Big Data refers to inconsistencies and uncertainty in data?
questions.explication: Veracity = inconsistencies and uncertainty. Variety = formats, velocity = speed, value = extracting useful data.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: Which V of Big Data describes the high speed of accumulation of data?
questions.explication: Velocity is the speed at which data accumulates; volume is the huge amount.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: Which V of Big Data means different formats of data from various sources?
questions.explication: Variety covers the different formats of data coming from various sources.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Data science and big data
questions.question: In the data-science Venn diagram, which field lies at the crossing of computer science and maths/statistics?
questions.explication: Machine learning = computer science + maths/statistics; traditional research = maths + domain; software development = computer science + domain.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: According to the course, machine learning lets computers perform tasks:
choix: Only by following rules written in advance by a programmer
Without explicit instructions, relying on patterns in data
Without any data, using only mathematical equations
Only after a human has labelled every possible input
questions.explication: ML is a subset of AI that enables computers to perform tasks without explicit instructions, relying on patterns and inference from data.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: In machine learning, what are the inputs given to the computer during learning?
choix: Data and output, producing a program or model
A program only, producing the data
The output only, producing the data
Data and a program, producing the output
questions.explication: Traditional programming: data + program -> output. Machine learning: data + output -> program/model.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Learning to recognise cars from images of cars and non-cars is:
questions.explication: The images come with correct answers (car / non-car): labelled data, so supervised learning.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Grouping stars or genomic data when no labels are given is:
questions.explication: Discovering hidden patterns in unlabelled data (clustering, grouping) is unsupervised learning.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Learning to play table tennis from occasional rewards after a series of decisions is:
questions.explication: Reinforcement learning: occasional rewards or punishments after a series of decisions.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Supervised methods are also called:
questions.explication: Supervised = predictive (predict an unknown value). Unsupervised = descriptive (find meaningful patterns).

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Predicting a patient's blood pressure is which supervised task?
questions.explication: Blood pressure is a numerical value, so the task is regression.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: What does supervised anomaly detection require?
choix: A reward signal sent after each action
Unlabelled data where most instances are normal
Training data labelled as normal and abnormal
questions.explication: Supervised anomaly detection uses data labelled 'normal' and 'abnormal' and involves training a classifier.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Unsupervised anomaly detection relies on which assumption?
choix: The majority of the instances are normal
The data follows a perfectly linear relationship
Anomalies form the largest cluster in the data
Every instance carries a normal or abnormal label
questions.explication: It detects anomalies in unlabelled data under the assumption that the majority of the instances are normal.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Product recommendations and store shelf management are typical applications of:
questions.explication: Association rule discovery finds human-interpretable associations, e.g. product recommendations.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Which unsupervised method describes the sequential dependencies among different events?
questions.explication: Sequential pattern discovery (buying patterns, gene sequencing) describes sequential dependencies among events.

questions.theme: Ch1 · Machine learning and its types
questions.question: Combining clustering and classification is called a:
questions.explication: The course notes that it is common to combine methods such as clustering and classification: hybrid methods.

questions.question: In reinforcement learning, what does the agent try to maximise?
choix: The accuracy on a labelled test set
questions.explication: RL is concerned with how agents take actions in an environment to maximize some notion of cumulative reward.

questions.question: In reinforcement learning, what is the 'state'?
choix: The set of all possible moves the agent can make
A representation of the agent's current situation
The external system the agent interacts with
The feedback received after each action taken
questions.explication: State = current situation of the agent. Actions = possible moves. Reward = feedback. Environment = external system.

questions.question: Which statement about the reward in reinforcement learning is correct?
choix: It is the label of each example
It is given before each action
It can be positive or negative
questions.explication: The reward is feedback from the environment based on the action; it can be positive or negative.

questions.question: How does a reinforcement learning agent improve over time?
choix: By clustering past states without any feedback at all
By trial and error, using feedback from its own actions
By solving the problem analytically in a single step
By copying labels supplied for every training example
questions.explication: The agent interacts with the environment in a trial-and-error manner, using feedback from its own actions and experiences.

questions.question: Which statement matches the course about statistical models versus ML?
choix: Machine learning requires the modeller to fix every relation first
Statistical models need no understanding of the variables involved
More assumptions in a predictive model give higher predictive power
Fewer assumptions in a predictive model give higher predictive power
questions.explication: The course states: the lesser the assumptions in a predictive model, the higher the predictive power.

questions.question: Statistical models are described in the course as:
choix: Based on storing training instances and comparing distances
Free of assumptions and based on iterative pattern search
Mathematics intensive and based on coefficient estimation
Requiring minimal human effort and no prior understanding
questions.explication: Statistical models are mathematics intensive, based on coefficient estimation, and require understanding the relations between variables first.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the linear regression assumptions listed in the statistical modelling slide?
choix: Homoscedasticity of the error term across values
Normally distributed error for each value
Independent variables must all be categorical
questions.explication: The listed assumptions are linearity, homoscedasticity, mean error of zero, independence of observations and normally distributed error.

questions.question: What does Python use to indicate a block of code?
questions.explication: Indentation (spaces at the start of a line) is very important in Python: it indicates a block of code.
questions.piege: A missing indentation is not a style issue: it raises an IndentationError.

questions.question: What does 'dynamically typed' mean for Python?
choix: Types are checked only by an external compiler
The type of a variable is inferred at runtime
Variables can never change their value once set
Every variable type must be declared in advance
questions.explication: You don't need to declare the type of a variable; it is inferred at runtime.

questions.question: Which variable name is valid in Python?
questions.explication: A name must start with a letter or underscore, cannot start with a digit, and only contains letters, digits and underscores.

questions.question: Are `name`, `Name` and `NAME` the same variable in Python?
choix: Only name and Name are the same
Yes, Python ignores the case of names
No, they are three different variables
Only Name and NAME are the same
questions.explication: Variable names are case-sensitive: name, Name and NAME are three different variables.

questions.question: Which symbol starts a single-line comment in Python?
questions.explication: A single-line comment starts with #. Multi-line comments/docstrings use triple quotes.

questions.question: What is printed by `print(x + y + z)` with x = "Python ", y = "is ", z = "awesome"?
questions.explication: The + operator concatenates strings without adding spaces; the spaces come from the strings themselves.

questions.question: What type of value does `input()` return?
questions.explication: input() always returns a string; convert it with int() or float() if you need a number.

questions.question: What is the value of `2 + 3 * 2 ** 2`?
questions.explication: Exponent first (2**2 = 4), then multiplication (3*4 = 12), then addition: 14.

questions.question: What is the value of `-2 ** 2` in Python?
questions.explication: ** has higher precedence than the unary minus, so it is -(2**2) = -4.
questions.piege: Many students answer 4: the exponent is applied before the unary minus.

questions.question: Which operator has the LOWEST precedence among these?
questions.explication: From high to low: comparisons, not, and, or.

questions.question: What does `7 // 2` return?
questions.explication: // is floor division: 7 // 2 = 3. The remainder 7 % 2 = 1.

questions.question: Which collection is ordered and unchangeable?
questions.explication: Tuple: ordered, unchangeable, allows duplicates. List: ordered and changeable.

questions.question: Which collection does not allow duplicates and is unindexed?
questions.explication: A set is unordered, unindexed and has no duplicates: {1, 2, 2, 3} gives {1, 2, 3}.

questions.question: With `marks = {"maths": 86, "science": 82}`, what does `marks["maths"]` return?
questions.explication: A dictionary is accessed by key: marks['maths'] returns the value 86.

questions.question: How many numbers does `for i in range(1, 11): print(i)` print?
questions.explication: range(1, 11) gives 1 to 10: the end value 11 is excluded.
questions.piege: range stops before its end value: range(1, 10) only goes up to 9.

questions.question: Which are the three types of flow control in Python listed in the course?
questions.explication: Conditional (if, if-else, if-elif-else, nested), iterative (for, while), transfer (break, continue, pass).

questions.question: Which of these is a transfer statement?
questions.explication: Transfer statements are break, continue and pass.

questions.question: What does the course's while loop summing i from 1 to 10 print?
With `def my_function(name = "Mafas")`, what does `my_function()` print?
questions.explication: "Mafas" is a default parameter value, used when no argument is passed.

questions.question: Which keyword defines a function in Python?
questions.explication: In Python a function is defined using the def keyword.

questions.question: Which pandas function reads a CSV file?
questions.explication: Readers follow the pattern read_xxx: read_csv, read_excel, read_json...

questions.question: What does `data.head()` display by default?
questions.explication: head() shows the first 5 rows, tail() the last 5.

questions.question: Which attribute gives the dimension (rows, columns) of a DataFrame?
questions.explication: shape gives the dimension; len(data) the number of records; columns the column list; dtypes the types.

questions.question: Which statistic is NOT part of the output of `describe()` on a numeric column?
questions.explication: describe() gives count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max. The mode comes from .mode().

questions.question: Which call summarises a categorical column by counting each category?
questions.explication: value_counts() gives the number of records per category.

questions.question: Which line counts the missing values in each column?
questions.explication: isnull() marks missing values as True; sum() counts them per column.

questions.question: In `data.drop('RowNumber', axis=1)`, what does `axis=1` mean?
questions.explication: axis=1 refers to columns, axis=0 to rows.
questions.piege: Without axis=1, pandas looks for a row label called 'RowNumber' and fails.

questions.question: What does `random_state=1` in `data.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=1)` ensure?
choix: Exactly one row is returned from the dataset
The same random sample is drawn on every run
The sample keeps the class proportions
Half of the columns are randomly selected
questions.explication: random_state fixes the random generator so the sampling is reproducible.

questions.question: Which merge type does pandas use by default?
questions.explication: Pandas uses an inner merge by default: only keys present in both dataframes are kept.

questions.question: Which merge keeps every row of the left dataframe and adds NaN where there is no match?
questions.explication: A left merge keeps every row of the left dataframe, with NaN where the key is missing on the right.

questions.question: data_1 has X1 = A, B, C and data_2 has X1 = A, B, D. How many rows does an outer merge on X1 give?
questions.explication: Outer keeps all keys from both sides: A, B, C, D, with NaN where there is no match.

questions.question: Same data (X1 = A, B, C and A, B, D). How many rows does the default merge give?
questions.explication: Default = inner: only the common keys A and B.

questions.question: What is the main difference between `pd.concat` and `pd.merge`?
choix: concat removes duplicates; merge always keeps every duplicate
concat works on Series only; merge works on DataFrames only
concat joins on shared columns; merge only stacks frames by rows
concat stacks frames; merge joins them on shared column values
questions.explication: Concat stacks data frames along rows or columns; merge combines them based on values in shared columns.

questions.question: Which library does the course describe as a 2D plotting library producing publication-quality figures?
questions.explication: Matplotlib is a Python 2D plotting library producing publication-quality figures.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the Matplotlib workflow?
choix: Prepare, create, plot, customize, save, show
Create, prepare, plot, show, customize, save
Prepare, plot, create, show, save, customize
Plot, prepare, create, save, customize, show
questions.explication: The six basic steps: 1 prepare data, 2 create plot, 3 plot, 4 customize, 5 save, 6 show.

questions.question: What is Seaborn?
choix: A data loading library that replaces pandas
A library built on Matplotlib for statistical graphics
A deep learning API running on top of TensorFlow
questions.explication: Seaborn is based on Matplotlib and provides a high-level interface for attractive statistical graphics.

questions.question: Which pandas call draws a univariate histogram of Age?
questions.explication: data['Age'].plot.hist() is univariate; data.plot.scatter(x=..., y=...) is bivariate.

questions.question: Which library does the course list for pre-processing, data split, modelling and evaluation of classical ML models?
questions.explication: Scikit-learn covers pre-processing, data split, modelling and evaluation (TensorFlow/Keras too, for deep learning).

questions.question: Which scikit-learn function splits data into training and test sets?
questions.explication: train_test_split(X, y, test_size=..., random_state=...) is in sklearn.model_selection.

questions.question: In the scikit-learn basic example, on which data is the StandardScaler fitted?
questions.explication: scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train), then transform both X_train and X_test.

questions.question: Which scikit-learn tool searches every combination of a hyperparameter grid?
questions.explication: GridSearchCV tries every combination in param_grid; RandomizedSearchCV samples n_iter combinations.

questions.question: In Keras, which last layer and loss suit a binary classification MLP?
questions.explication: Binary: sigmoid + binary_crossentropy. Multi-class: softmax + categorical_crossentropy. Regression: linear output + mse.

questions.question: In the Keras cheat sheet, which compile setting is used for an MLP regression?
questions.explication: For regression: model.compile(optimizer='rmsprop', loss='mse', metrics=['mae']).

questions.question: Supervised learning is a type of machine learning where the model is trained on:
questions.explication: Supervised learning trains the model on labelled data: inputs paired with the correct output.

questions.question: In supervised learning, the features are:
choix: The internal parameters learned by the model
The metrics used to evaluate the predictions
The input variables used to make predictions
The desired outcomes the model must predict
questions.explication: Features = inputs. Labels/targets = outputs, the desired prediction outcomes.

questions.question: Predicting house prices from size and location is:
questions.explication: The price is a continuous value, so it is regression.

questions.question: Classifying fruit as apples or strawberries is:
questions.explication: The label is discrete (apple / strawberry), so it is classification.

questions.question: The Iris data set has three labels (Setosa, Versicolour, Virginica). This target is:
questions.explication: Three possible classes: a multilevel (multi-class) target.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an attribute of the Iris data set?
questions.explication: The four Iris attributes are sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width (cm).

questions.question: The Forest Fires data set was originally a regression task. What turns it into binary classification?
choix: Keeping only the spatial coordinates X and Y
Removing the meteorological attributes from the data
Grouping the months into four seasons
Predicting 'burned area or not' instead of the area
questions.explication: The original target is the burned area (regression). Using 'burned or not' (0/1) makes the target binary.

questions.question: In the supervised learning diagram, what makes up the 'generalization' phase?
choix: Clustering the test data before any prediction is made
Feeding training data and training labels into the model
Predicting the test data and evaluating against test labels
Collecting more labels for the training set
questions.explication: Training/building = training data + labels -> model. Generalization = test data -> prediction -> evaluation with test labels.

questions.question: Why is the model evaluated on test data rather than training data?
choix: To make the training of the model run faster
Because the test set is always larger than the training set
Because training data cannot be used to make predictions
To measure how it performs on new, unseen data
questions.explication: The goal is to predict new cases; scoring on training data measures memorisation, not generalization.

questions.question: What are the steps of the cat versus dog learning pipeline?
choix: Design features, define task, test, collect data, train
Collect data, train, define task, test, design features
Define task, collect data, design features, train, test
Train, test, define task, design features, collect data
questions.explication: 0 define task, 1 collect data, 2 design features, 3 train model, 4 test model.

questions.question: How does the course define overfitting?
choix: The model is trained on too few features to make predictions
The model learns noise and details that hurt performance on new data
The model is too simple to capture the patterns in the data
The model is evaluated on the training set instead of test data
questions.explication: Overfitting: the model learns noise and details in the training data, which negatively impacts performance on new data.

questions.question: How does the course define underfitting?
choix: The model memorises the noise contained in the training set
The model performs well on training data but badly on test data
The model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns
The model uses too many hidden layers and features
questions.explication: Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the data.

questions.question: What is the 'model' in the course's key terminology?
choix: The output or target variable to be predicted
The set of input variables fed to the system
The dataset used to evaluate the predictions
questions.explication: Model: the mathematical representation of the learning process.

questions.question: Which is listed as a challenge of supervised learning?
choix: Too few algorithms to choose from
Total absence of any labelled data
questions.explication: Challenges: data quality, bias and variance, computational cost, interpretability, ethical concerns.

questions.question: Sentiment analysis of customer reviews is listed as an application of:
questions.explication: Applications of supervised learning: spam detection, medical diagnosis, sentiment analysis, fraud detection, image classification.

questions.question: In the pipeline, what comes right after 'Problem + Dataset'?
questions.explication: Order: problem + dataset, data understanding, data cleaning, data split, preprocessing, model building, tuning, evaluation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the data understanding step?
choix: To deploy the model on new streaming data
To choose the final hyperparameters of the model
To detect noise such as missing values and outliers
To split the data into train and test subsets
questions.explication: Data understanding detects noise: missing values, outliers, non-normal distributions, duplicates, inconsistent data.

questions.question: According to the course, roughly how much of a data science project's time does preprocessing consume?
questions.explication: Data preprocessing is a crucial task that can consume 80% of the total project time.

questions.question: How must categorical data be handled in preprocessing?
questions.explication: Categorical data must be encoded. Class balancing uses under- or oversampling.

questions.question: Which treatment does the course list for class balancing?
questions.explication: Class balancing -> undersampling or oversampling. Feature selection -> correlation, Chi2, R square test.

questions.question: Which techniques are listed for feature selection?
choix: Correlation, Chi2 test, R square test
questions.explication: Feature selection: correlation, Chi2 test, R square test.

questions.question: Which tools does the pipeline name for hyperparameter tuning?
questions.explication: Hyperparameter tuning uses Grid SearchCV or Randomized SearchCV, giving the tuned model.

questions.question: How is the ML algorithm chosen in the model building step?
choix: From the size of the test set only
Always by picking the most complex model available
By using the first algorithm listed in scikit-learn
From literature review and past work experience
questions.explication: Algorithm selection is based on literature review and past work experience; usually several models are built and compared.

questions.question: In the pipeline, what is the 'base model'?
choix: A model trained on the test data for comparison
The first model built with default hyperparameters
The model retrained on all the data at the end
The model obtained after hyperparameter tuning
questions.explication: The ML model building step produces a base model with default HPs; tuning then produces the tuned model.

questions.question: Which operation is safe to perform BEFORE the train-test split?
questions.explication: Before the split: only operations based on domain knowledge or predefined rules (remove irrelevant features, duplicates, fix corrupted data, type conversion).

questions.question: Which operation must be done AFTER the split, fitted on training data only?
questions.explication: Scaling uses mean and std learned from data, so it must be fitted on training data only.

questions.question: Why must SMOTE / class weights be applied after the split?
choix: They must not expose the test distribution
They remove duplicates from both datasets
They are based on predefined domain rules
They only work on numeric categorical data
questions.explication: Class imbalance handling must not expose the test distribution: train data only.

questions.question: What is data leakage?
choix: Missing values appearing after merging two dataframes
Test-set information used during training or preprocessing
Overfitting caused by having far too many training rows
Rows lost when the dataset is split into separate subsets
questions.explication: Data leakage = test information influences training, which makes the test score too optimistic.

questions.question: What is the correct way to scale train and test data?
choix: Fit on all data before splitting, then transform
Fit and transform train and test separately
Fit on train, then transform both train and test
Fit on test, then transform both train and test
questions.explication: Fit on training data only, save the parameters, transform both sets. Never recalculate statistics on the test set.
questions.piege: fit_transform on the full dataset before the split is data leakage.

questions.question: Train ages are 20, 30, 40 (mean 30, std about 8.16). What is the correct z-score of a test age of 50?
questions.explication: z = (50 - 30) / 8.16 = 2.45, using the training mean and std. Recomputing the mean on the test point would wrongly give 0.

questions.question: What is the course's ground rule for the train-test split?
questions.explication: Ground rule: train > test (50/50, 60/40, 70/30, 80/20), but an equal split is possible if the dataset size is OK.

questions.question: With 1,000 rows and an 80/20 split, how many test rows are there?
questions.explication: 80% train = 800 rows, 20% test = 200 rows.

questions.question: How does the course define bias?
choix: The number of parameters inside a model
The variation among fits of different samples
The proportion of variance explained by a model
The error in fitting a model
questions.explication: Bias is the error in fitting a model. Variance is the variation among fits of different training samples.

questions.question: How does the course define variance?
choix: Variation among fits of different samples of one population
The gap between the training error and the test error
The error between the fitted model and the training points
The spread of the target variable around its mean value
questions.explication: Variance is the measure of variation among the fits of different sample training sets on the same population.

questions.question: What happens when model complexity increases?
questions.explication: Increasing complexity decreases bias but increases variance: the bias-variance trade-off.

questions.question: Which pattern indicates a high bias problem?
choix: Low training error, low test error
Low training error, very high test error
High training error, test error similar to it
High training error, much lower test error
questions.explication: High bias: high training error and a validation/test error of similar magnitude.

questions.question: A model has 2% training error and 20% validation error. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explication: Low training error and very high validation error = high variance.

questions.question: Which action is listed in the course to decrease bias?
choix: Reduce the number of features in the model
Stop the training process much earlier
Increase model complexity, e.g. more features
Switch to a simpler linear model instead
questions.explication: To decrease bias: more training data may help; increase complexity (more features, nonlinear models, more hidden layers).
questions.piege: More data mainly helps high variance; against high bias the main lever is more complexity.

questions.question: On the error vs model complexity curve, where is the best model?
choix: At the minimum of the training error
At the minimum of the validation error
questions.explication: Training error keeps falling; validation error falls then rises. The best model is at the minimum of validation error.

questions.question: What is regularization in the course?
choix: Splitting the data into k folds of exactly equal size
Scaling every feature to the same numeric range first
Removing duplicate rows before the train-test split
Relaxing an overfit model so it represents the population
questions.explication: If the model is overfit to the sample it may not represent the population; relaxing it is called regularization.

questions.question: Which optimisation techniques does the training summary mention?
questions.explication: Training and optimization: the model adjusts its parameters with techniques like SGD or Adam to minimize a loss.

questions.question: A false positive is:
choix: An actual positive predicted as positive
An actual negative predicted as positive
An actual positive predicted as negative
An actual negative predicted as negative
questions.explication: FP = false alarm: actually negative, predicted positive. FN = miss: actually positive, predicted negative.

questions.question: A false negative is:
choix: An actual negative predicted as negative
An actual positive predicted as negative
An actual negative predicted as positive
An actual positive predicted as positive
questions.explication: FN = miss: the model says negative but the case was positive.

questions.question: In scikit-learn, `confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)` puts what in the rows?
questions.explication: scikit-learn: rows = actual (true) labels, columns = predicted labels.
questions.piege: The course shows two layouts; always read the axis titles. The heatmap slide swaps the axis labels.

questions.question: A heatmap shows row 0 = [58, 0] and row 1 = [22, 0], rows being actual labels. What is the model doing?
choix: Predicting each class half the time
questions.explication: Column 1 is empty: no case was ever predicted as 1. The model predicts 0 for everyone.

questions.question: Which formula gives accuracy?
questions.explication: Accuracy = correct predictions / all predictions.

questions.question: When is accuracy the best metric, according to the course?
questions.explication: Accuracy is best when the classes are balanced.

questions.question: If accuracy is 0.85, what is the error rate?
questions.explication: ERR = 1 - ACC = 0.15.

questions.question: Which formula gives precision?
questions.explication: Precision = true positives / all positive predictions.
questions.piege: Precision divides by predicted positives (TP+FP); recall divides by actual positives (TP+FN).

questions.question: Which formula gives recall?
questions.explication: Recall = true positives / all actual positives. It is also the true positive rate.

questions.question: Precision is especially important when:
choix: The cost of false negatives is high
The cost of false positives is high
questions.explication: Precision matters when false positives are costly; recall when false negatives are costly.

questions.question: For cancer screening, where missing a sick patient is very costly, which metric should be favoured?
questions.explication: A missed patient is a false negative: favour recall.

questions.question: For a spam filter, where sending a good e-mail to spam is costly, which metric should be favoured?
questions.explication: A good mail flagged as spam is a false positive: favour precision.

questions.question: How is the F1 score defined?
choix: The difference between recall and precision
The arithmetic mean of accuracy and recall
The harmonic mean of precision and recall
The product of precision and recall
questions.explication: F1 = 2 x (P x R) / (P + R), the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

questions.question: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130. What is the precision?
TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130. What is the recall?
TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 130. What is the accuracy?
Precision = 0.80 and recall = 0.667. What is the F1 score (approximately)?
In a classification report, how is the 'macro avg' computed?
choix: Score of the majority class only
Plain mean of the per-class scores
Mean weighted by the class support
questions.explication: Macro average = simple mean over classes; weighted average weights each class by its support.

questions.question: A model has 73% accuracy but precision and recall of 0 for class 1. What does this show?
choix: Class 1 has more support than class 0
Accuracy hides that the model never finds class 1
The report contains a calculation error
The model is reliable for both of the classes
questions.explication: On unbalanced data, a model predicting only the majority class can have good accuracy and be useless for the minority class.

questions.question: What does the ROC curve plot?
choix: True positive rate vs false positive rate
Precision against recall at each threshold
questions.explication: ROC: TP rate (recall) on the y-axis against FP rate (1 - specificity) on the x-axis, at various thresholds.

questions.question: On a ROC curve, the diagonal line corresponds to:
questions.explication: Diagonal = random guessing; below it, predictions are opposite of the true class.

questions.question: Which (TP rate, FP rate) point is ideal?
questions.explication: (1,0): all positives found, no false alarm. (0,0): everything negative. (1,1): everything positive.

questions.question: What does the point (TP rate, FP rate) = (1, 1) mean?
choix: Declaring everything to be the positive class
Declaring everything to be the negative class
questions.explication: At (1,1) every case is predicted positive: all positives are found but every negative is a false alarm.

questions.question: What AUC value corresponds to random guessing?
questions.explication: AUC = 1 is perfect, 0.5 is random guessing.

questions.question: At threshold t, TPR = 0.5 and FPR = 0.12. What is the true negative rate?
questions.explication: TNR = 1 - FPR = 0.88 (the slide mislabels it as FN).

questions.question: What changes the location of a classifier's point on the ROC curve?
choix: Only the number of features that are used
Only the choice of the evaluation metric
Only the size of the training set provided
Threshold, sample distribution or cost matrix
questions.explication: Changing the threshold of the algorithm, the sample distribution or the cost matrix changes the location of the point.

questions.question: Which formula gives the MAE?
questions.explication: MAE = mean of absolute differences between predicted and actual values.

questions.question: Which regression metric penalises larger errors more heavily?
questions.explication: MSE squares the errors, so big errors weigh much more.

questions.question: Why is RMSE often easier to interpret than MSE?
choix: It ignores the very largest errors
It has the same units as the target
It is always smaller than the MAE value
questions.explication: RMSE = √MSE keeps the units of the target variable.

questions.question: y = (3, 5, 2, 7) and ŷ = (2.5, 5, 4, 8). What is the MAE?
y = (3, 5, 2, 7) and ŷ = (2.5, 5, 4, 8). What is the MSE?
Which scikit-learn call computes the RMSE?
questions.explication: RMSE = square root of the MSE.

questions.question: Why does the argument order matter in `r2_score`?
choix: It does not matter for any sklearn metric
R² is not symmetric: true values come first
It also changes the sign of the MAE value
questions.explication: The signature is (y_true, y_pred). For MAE/MSE the order does not change the value, for R² it does.

questions.question: What is adjusted R² useful for?
choix: Comparing models with different predictor counts
Evaluating binary classifiers on unbalanced data
Measuring errors in the target variable's units
Choosing the best classification threshold value
questions.explication: Adjusted R² adjusts R² for the number of predictors.

questions.question: In adjusted R² = 1 - (1 - R²)(N - 1)/(N - k - 1), what is k?
questions.explication: N is the sample size and k the number of predictors (written n and p in the regression chapter).

questions.question: Which principle of metric choice means using several metrics to see performance from different angles?
questions.explication: Relevance: align with objectives. Diversity: variety of metrics. Contextualization: consider data and domain.

questions.question: How does the course define cross-validation?
choix: A preprocessing step that scales features to a common range
An optimisation algorithm that minimises the cost function
A resampling procedure to evaluate models on a limited data sample
A method that removes duplicates before the data split
questions.explication: Cross-validation is a resampling procedure used to evaluate ML models on a limited data sample.

questions.question: Why are cross-validation methods needed?
choix: They replace the need for a separate evaluation metric
Models cannot be trained without first using k-fold splits
We rarely have enough samples to represent the whole population
They remove the need to preprocess categorical data
questions.explication: In most cases we lack a large number of samples; CV makes the best use of them so the model represents the population.

questions.question: Which three cross-validation techniques does the course list?
questions.explication: Holdout cross validation, K-fold cross validation, Nested/Repeated cross validation.

questions.question: In k-fold cross-validation, how many folds are used for training in each iteration?
questions.explication: The model is trained on k-1 folds and tested on the remaining one, k times.

questions.question: How is the final k-fold performance obtained?
choix: By averaging the k fold performances
By summing the k fold scores
By keeping the best fold's score
By keeping the last fold's score
questions.explication: Performance = (1/k) Σ Performance_i.

questions.question: In 5-fold CV on 1,000 rows, how many rows train each model?
questions.explication: Each fold has 200 rows; each model trains on 4 folds = 800 rows.

questions.question: 5-fold accuracies are 0.82, 0.85, 0.80, 0.84, 0.83. What is the CV accuracy?
What does '5-fold cross-validation' mean?
choix: The model is trained 5 times on all data
k = 5: the data is split into 5 groups
5% of the data is used for testing
questions.explication: The parameter k is the number of groups; k = 5 becomes 5-fold cross-validation.

questions.question: Stratified cross-validation is used for:
questions.explication: Stratified CV is used for classification problems.

questions.question: What does stratified k-fold guarantee?
choix: Each fold is used twice as the validation fold
Each fold is sorted by the value of the target
Each fold contains exactly the same number of features
Each fold keeps roughly the same class proportions
questions.explication: Stratified k-fold selects folds so that each contains roughly the same proportions of class labels.

questions.question: 1,000 rows with 30% positives, stratified 5-fold. About how many positives per fold?
questions.explication: Each fold has 200 rows; 30% of 200 = 60 positives.

questions.question: In holdout cross-validation, what is the validation set used for?
questions.explication: Models with different hyperparameters are compared on the validation set; the test set gives the final estimate.

questions.question: In holdout CV, why is the validation score slightly optimistic?
choix: The validation set is used to train the final model
The validation set is always larger than the test set
The validation set has no labels to compare with
The hyperparameters were chosen to fit the validation set
questions.explication: Choosing hyperparameters on the validation set tunes the model to it, so the untouched test set gives the honest score.

questions.question: In the last step of holdout and k-fold CV, the final model is trained on:
choix: All data, with the best hyperparameters
The test set only, with the best values
A single random fold, with the defaults
The validation set only, with defaults
questions.explication: Final step: retrain the learning algorithm with the best hyperparameters on all data and labels.

questions.question: What does nested cross-validation do?
choix: Tunes in an inner CV loop and estimates performance in an outer loop
Uses the test set to tune hyperparameters inside every fold
Splits the data into nested clusters before classification
Repeats one train-test split with the same random seed many times
questions.explication: Nested CV places a tuning CV loop inside an evaluation CV loop, so tuning never sees the data used for the score.

questions.question: Besides validation, what does cross-validation help with according to the course?
questions.explication: It helps balance bias and variance, reducing overfitting or underfitting.

questions.question: KNN can be used for:
questions.explication: KNN is used for classification (vote) and regression (average).

questions.question: Why is KNN called a lazy learning algorithm?
choix: It trains slowly over many epochs with a small learning rate
It memorises the training data instead of learning a function
It postpones data preprocessing until after prediction
It only uses a small random part of the training data
questions.explication: KNN doesn't learn a discriminative function; it memorizes the training dataset.

questions.question: What does 'non-parametric' mean for KNN?
choix: It cannot use numeric features as its input
It requires the data to be normally distributed
It has no hyperparameter at all to be tuned
It assumes nothing about the data distribution
questions.explication: Non-parametric: KNN makes no assumptions about the underlying data distribution.

questions.question: In KNN classification, how is the class of the query point decided?
choix: Label of one randomly chosen training point
Majority vote among the k nearest neighbours
Label of the farthest of the k neighbours
Average of the labels of all training points
questions.explication: Classification: majority vote. Regression: average of the neighbours' target values.

questions.question: In KNN regression, what is the predicted value?
choix: Target value of the single farthest neighbour
Mean target value of the k nearest neighbours
Most frequent target value in the whole dataset
Median target value of all the training points
questions.explication: Regression follows the same steps but averages the target values of the k nearest neighbours.

questions.question: What happens in KNN's training phase?
choix: It computes the weights of a line
It just stores the training data
questions.explication: The algorithm doesn't explicitly train a model; it stores the training data.

questions.question: Which is listed as a con of KNN?
choix: It cannot be used for any regression
A very long and costly training phase
It is too hard to understand or code
questions.explication: Cons: expensive prediction, depends on k and distance, sensitive to irrelevant features, curse of dimensionality.

questions.question: Why is KNN prediction expensive on large datasets?
choix: Each query runs a full cross-validation of the model
Each query must first normalise the whole test set
Each query needs its distance to every training point
Each query retrains the model from scratch on all data
questions.explication: Lazy learning moves the work to prediction: one distance per training point for every query.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as a pro of KNN?
choix: No training phase besides storing data
questions.explication: KNN is sensitive to irrelevant or redundant features: that is a con.

questions.question: Which formula is the Euclidean distance?
questions.explication: Euclidean = square root of the sum of squared differences. Manhattan = sum of absolute differences.

questions.question: Minkowski distance with p = 1 is equal to:
questions.explication: Minkowski (Σ|x_i - y_i|^p)^(1/p): p = 1 gives Manhattan, p = 2 gives Euclidean.

questions.question: Minkowski distance with p = 2 is equal to:
questions.explication: p = 2 gives the Euclidean distance.

questions.question: What is the Manhattan distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
questions.explication: |4 - 1| + |6 - 2| = 3 + 4 = 7. The Euclidean distance is 5.

questions.question: What is the Euclidean distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
What is the Euclidean distance between (5, 4) and (6, 5)?
Training points: (2,3) A, (1,1) B, (4,2) A, (6,5) B, (7,8) B. With k = 3 and Euclidean distance, how is (5, 4) classified?
choix: A tie between A and B
questions.explication: Nearest: (6,5) B at 1.41, (4,2) A at 2.24, (2,3) A at 3.16. Vote B, A, A -> A.
questions.piege: The single nearest point is B, but with k = 3 the majority vote gives A.

questions.question: Same training points, query (5, 4). How is it classified with k = 1?
choix: It depends on the metric only
questions.explication: With k = 1 only the nearest point (6,5), label B, votes.

questions.question: Same training points, query (5, 4). How is it classified with k = 5?
questions.explication: All 5 points vote: A, A, B, B, B -> B. The prediction depends on k.

questions.question: What does a small k tend to cause in KNN?
questions.explication: Small k: complex boundary, overfitting. Large k: smoother boundary, underfitting.

questions.question: A larger value of k gives:
choix: More complex models that overfit the data
Smoother boundaries and less complex models
Exactly the same boundary as with k = 1
Faster predictions on very large datasets
questions.explication: Larger k means smoother curves of separation, resulting in less complex models.

questions.question: How does the course recommend choosing k?
choix: Always k equal to the dataset size
questions.explication: k is a crucial hyperparameter that can be chosen using cross-validation.

questions.question: Why choose an odd k for binary classification?
choix: Because even k is not allowed
To avoid ties in the vote
questions.explication: With two classes, an odd k prevents a 2-2 style tie in the majority vote.

questions.question: Why is normalization strongly recommended for KNN?
choix: KNN cannot read non-normalized values at all
Normalization removes the need to choose k
Features with larger ranges dominate the distances
questions.explication: KNN relies on distances; features on large scales (e.g. income) dominate smaller ones (e.g. age).

questions.question: According to the course, is normalization mathematically mandatory for KNN?
choix: No, but it is strongly recommended
Yes, KNN cannot run without it
questions.explication: Normalization is not mathematically mandatory, but it is strongly recommended for both KNN classifier and regressor.

questions.question: Age ranges 18-60 and income 20,000-200,000. Without scaling, which feature dominates the Euclidean distance?
questions.explication: Income differences are in thousands, age differences in tens: income dominates.

questions.question: Which class implements KNN classification in scikit-learn?
questions.explication: from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier; KNeighborsRegressor is for regression.

questions.question: What is the default number of neighbours of `KNeighborsClassifier()`?
questions.explication: scikit-learn's default n_neighbors is 5.

questions.question: A numeric continuous target calls for:
questions.explication: Numeric continuous target -> estimation -> linear regression. Binary target -> logistic regression.

questions.question: A binary target calls for:
questions.explication: Binary/discrete valued target -> classification/decision -> logistic regression.

questions.question: Simple linear regression uses:
questions.explication: Simple: 1 IV and 1 TV. Multiple: >1 IV, 1 TV. Multivariate: >1 IV, >1 TV.

questions.question: Multivariate linear regression assumes:
choix: An input vector with exactly one target
A single input with a single output
An output vector: several target variables
A polynomial relation of degree n
questions.explication: Multivariate = output vector y = (y1, ..., yn): more than one target.
questions.piege: Multiple = several inputs; multivariate = several outputs.

questions.question: In y = w0 + w1x, what is w1?
questions.explication: w0 is the intercept (y when x = 0), w1 is the slope.

questions.question: What does RSS stand for?
questions.explication: RSS = Σ (y_actual - y_predicted)², a measure of the discrepancy between data and model.

questions.question: What does least squares minimise?
questions.explication: Least squares picks the line with the smallest RSS.

questions.question: x = (1, 2, 3, 4), y = (2, 4, 5, 8). What is the least-squares slope?
How are the weights of multiple linear regression found mathematically, according to the course?
choix: They are read off a scatter plot
They are set by k-fold CV
questions.explication: Mathematical solution to find multiple linear regression parameters requires matrix inversion, etc.

questions.question: Polynomial regression models the relation between x and y as:
questions.explication: Polynomial regression fits a curve: y modelled as an nth degree polynomial of x.

questions.question: Why is polynomial regression still a form of linear regression?
choix: It is linear in the weights; x² acts as a new feature
It uses the sigmoid function on the output
It always fits a straight line through the data
It only works with a single binary feature
questions.explication: y = b0 + b1x + b2x² is a curve in x but linear in the weights.

questions.question: Which assumption of linear regression means the residuals have constant variance?
questions.explication: Homoscedasticity: constant variance of residuals.

questions.question: Which is NOT an assumption of linear regression in the course?
questions.explication: The four assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality.

questions.question: Why must a linear model be assessed after fitting?
choix: Least squares gives a line even with no linear relation
The fitted line always passes through every data point
Least squares refuses to fit data that is not linear
The slope is always zero for real-world data
questions.explication: The least squares method produces a regression line whether or not there is a linear relationship.

questions.question: Four datasets (Anscombe's quartet) share almost the same regression line. What is the lesson?
choix: Always plot the data and residuals, not just statistics
Outliers never affect a least-squares regression line
R² alone proves that a linear model is appropriate
Linear regression suits any data with the same mean
questions.explication: Similar statistics can hide curves, outliers or leverage points; plotting reveals where linear regression is not suitable.

questions.question: How is R² interpreted?
choix: Number of predictors in the model
Proportion of variance in y predictable from x
Probability that a coefficient is zero
Average absolute error of the predictions
questions.explication: R² is the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable predictable from the independent variable(s).

questions.question: Which formula is correct?
questions.explication: R² = ESS/TSS = 1 - RSS/TSS, with TSS = ESS + RSS.

questions.question: TSS is defined as:
questions.explication: TSS = total sum of squares around the mean. RSS = Σ(y-ŷ)². ESS = Σ(ŷ-ȳ)².

questions.question: ESS (explained sum of squares) is:
questions.explication: ESS measures the variation explained by the model: predictions around the mean.

questions.question: An R² of 0.20 means:
choix: The slope of the fitted line is equal to 0.20
20% of the variance in Y is predictable from X
The model is 20% accurate on the test data
20% of all the predictions made are wrong
questions.explication: R² = 0.20 means 20 percent of the variance in Y is predictable from X.

questions.question: When can R² be negative?
choix: Never: R² always lies between 0 and 1
Only when the fitted slope is negative
When there are far too many observations
No intercept, or a fit worse than the mean
questions.explication: R² can be negative if the model has no intercept or fits worse than using the mean.
questions.piege: '0 < R² < 1' only holds on training data for a model with an intercept.

questions.question: What does R² = 0 mean for a model with an intercept?
choix: It explains all of the variance of y
The slope of the line is exactly 1
It explains none of the variance (ŷ = ȳ)
questions.explication: R² = 0: the model does no better than always predicting the mean.

questions.question: Does a high R² prove causation?
choix: Yes, an R² above 0.9 proves causation
Yes, provided the p-value is also high
No, a better fit does not prove causation
Only in the case of multiple regression
questions.explication: A higher R² indicates a better fit, but it does not guarantee causation.

questions.question: Adding a useless variable to a regression model usually:
choix: Raises adjusted R² but lowers R²
Lowers both R² and adjusted R²
Leaves R² exactly as it was before
Raises R² but can lower adjusted R²
questions.explication: R² never decreases when adding a variable; adjusted R² penalises each extra predictor.

questions.question: n = 50, p = 2, R² = 0.80. What is the adjusted R² (approximately)?
What does the F-statistic test in linear regression?
choix: The overall significance of the model
The size of the test set
questions.explication: F-statistic: overall significance (relationship between y and the set of IVs). t-tests: individual coefficients.

questions.question: What are t-tests used for in linear regression?
choix: Splitting the data into several folds
questions.explication: t-tests determine the significance of individual regression coefficients.

questions.question: Which scikit-learn class fits a linear regression?
questions.explication: from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression.

questions.question: What is gradient descent?
choix: A metric to evaluate regression models
A distance metric used by the KNN model
An algorithm that minimises a function
A method that splits data into k folds
questions.explication: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used to minimize a function, such as a cost function.

questions.question: Which cost function is usually used for linear regression in the course?
questions.explication: The difference between predicted and actual y is measured with a cost function, usually the MSE.

questions.question: Where are the best parameters located on the cost surface?
choix: At the origin of the axes
At the maximum of the cost function
On the edge of the surface
At the minimum of the cost function
questions.explication: The set of parameters giving the best performance is at the minimum of the cost surface.

questions.question: On the left of the minimum, the gradient is negative. What should gradient descent do to w?
questions.explication: Move in the negative of the gradient direction: negative gradient -> increase w; positive gradient -> decrease w.

questions.question: Which is the gradient descent update rule?
questions.explication: Subtract the gradient times the step length α.
questions.piege: Adding the gradient climbs towards a maximum.

questions.question: In gradient descent, what does the learning rate α control?
questions.explication: α is the fixed step length: big α makes large jumps, small α small steps.

questions.question: What can happen with a learning rate that is too big?
choix: The steps overshoot and may diverge
questions.explication: A big learning rate overshoots the minimum and can bounce or diverge; a small one is slow but reliable.

questions.question: Minimise g(w) = (w - 3)² with w0 = 0 and α = 0.1. What is w after one step?
Same function g(w) = (w - 3)², w0 = 0 but α = 1.1. What happens?
choix: It overshoots further each step and diverges
w stays at 0 because the gradient is zero
It reaches the minimum w = 3 in a single step
It converges slowly but surely towards w = 3
questions.explication: w1 = 6.6, w2 = -1.32, w3 = 8.18: each step overshoots more, the algorithm diverges.

questions.question: What is an epoch?
choix: One pass over all training samples
One fold of a cross-validation run
One update of a single model weight
questions.explication: Epoch: one set of presentation of all training samples to the model.

questions.question: In minibatch mode, what is presented before deciding on a weight update?
choix: A small set of training samples
questions.explication: Batch mode: all samples per update. Minibatch: a small set. Stochastic: one sample.

questions.question: With 1,000 samples and a batch size of 100, how many weight updates happen per epoch in mini-batch mode?
questions.explication: 1,000 / 100 = 10 updates per epoch. Batch GD gives 1, SGD gives 1,000.

questions.question: When can an optimum solution be found deterministically?
choix: If it can be modelled mathematically
When the cost has several local minima
When no cost function can be defined
When all the data in use is unlabelled
questions.explication: Deterministic: if the problem can be modelled mathematically. Otherwise, nondeterministic iterative search.

questions.question: Why can gradient descent be difficult on real-world cost functions?
questions.explication: Real-world problems are complex and may have several minima.

questions.question: Logistic regression is used for:
questions.explication: Despite its name, logistic regression is used for classification.
questions.piege: It is evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC/AUC, not with MSE or R².

questions.question: To decide the class of an instance, what matters about the score w0 + w1x1 + w2x2?
questions.explication: In deciding the class we are only interested in the sign of the score.

questions.question: What does the magnitude of the score tell us?
choix: How sure we are of the class
questions.explication: The larger the distance from the decision boundary, the surer the class.

questions.question: What does the sigmoid function do in logistic regression?
choix: Maps scores to probabilities between 0 and 1
Maps probabilities to counts for each class
Splits the dataset into two equal halves
Squares the score to get rid of its sign
questions.explication: P(y = +1 | x, w) = 1 / (1 + e^(-wᵀh(x))): the sigmoid maps the score to a probability.

questions.question: A score of 0 gives which probability P(y = +1)?
questions.explication: 1 / (1 + e^0) = 0.5: the point lies on the decision boundary.

questions.question: A score of 2 gives which probability P(y = +1), approximately?
A score of -1 gives which probability P(y = +1), approximately?
questions.explication: 1 / (1 + e^1) ≈ 0.269, so class -1 is predicted.

questions.question: As the score tends to +∞, the probability P(y = +1 | x) tends to:
questions.explication: Score -> +∞: very sure ŷ = +1, probability -> 1. Score -> -∞: probability -> 0.

questions.question: Where is the decision boundary of logistic regression?
questions.explication: Fit a linear boundary with wᵀh(x) = 0, where the probability is 0.5.

questions.question: In n dimensions, what does a linear classifier's boundary represent?
choix: One cluster centre for each of the classes
A curve that passes through every point
A hyperplane splitting space into two halves
A circle drawn around each separate class
questions.explication: In n dimensions, a linear classifier represents a hyperplane separating the space into two half-spaces.

questions.question: How is the ambiguity of points near the boundary expressed in logistic regression?
questions.explication: When classes overlap, the ambiguity of class assignment is expressed through probabilities.

questions.question: Which objective functions does the course mention for logistic regression?
choix: Mean squared, root mean squared, absolute error
Accuracy, precision, recall and the F1 score
Max likelihood, log likelihood, cross entropy
questions.explication: Maximum likelihood, log likelihood and cross entropy: effectively, all these functions mean the same.

questions.question: What is 'parameter tuning' in the course's central idea of ML?
choix: Finding parameters that optimise the objective
Renaming the features before training a model
Removing all outliers from the training data
Choosing which rows will go into the test set
questions.explication: An objective function reflecting performance is defined; parameters that optimize it are determined: parameter tuning.

questions.question: Which line is missing between `fit` and the metrics in the course's LinearRegression and LogisticRegression code?
questions.explication: The slides compute metrics on y_pred without creating it; y_pred = model.predict(x_test) is needed.
